Resistivity

QTrans evaluates phonon-limited metallic resistivity using either a transport Eliashberg spectral function or the conductivity tensor obtained from the Boltzmann transport equation (BTE).

Transport Eliashberg Spectral Function

The scalar spectral approach uses a Fermi-surface approximation and an isotropic description of transport. To fix the normalization, the formulas in this section refer to a nonmagnetic, spin-degenerate metal: \(N_F=N(\varepsilon_F)\) is the density of electronic states per unit cell, per unit energy, and per spin, and the band sums include one copy of each spin-degenerate band. The variable \(\omega\) denotes angular frequency, so the phonon energy is \(\hbar\omega\).

The Eliashberg spectral function is

\[\alpha^2F(\omega) = \frac{1}{2}\sum_b\int_{\mathrm{BZ}} \frac{d^3q}{\Omega_{\mathrm{BZ}}} \omega_{\mathbf{q}b}\lambda_{\mathbf{q}b} \delta(\omega-\omega_{\mathbf{q}b}),\]

where the mode-resolved electron-phonon coupling constant is

\[\lambda_{\mathbf{q}b} = \frac{2}{\hbar N_F\omega_{\mathbf{q}b}} \sum_{\mu\nu}\int_{\mathrm{BZ}}\frac{d^3k}{\Omega_{\mathrm{BZ}}} |g_{\mu\nu b}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q})|^2 \delta(\varepsilon_{\nu\mathbf{k}}-\varepsilon_F) \delta(\varepsilon_{\mu\mathbf{k+q}}-\varepsilon_F).\]

Here, \(\varepsilon_F\) is the Fermi energy, \(g_{\mu\nu b}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q})\) is an electron-phonon coupling matrix element with units of energy, and \(\Omega_{\mathrm{BZ}}\) is the Brillouin-zone volume. The factor of 2 accounts for spin degeneracy in a nonmagnetic system. For collinear spin-polarized calculations, each spin channel is treated separately, so this factor is 1. This distinction is handled explicitly in the code. These conventions give the dimensionless total coupling

\[\lambda = \sum_b\int_{\mathrm{BZ}}\frac{d^3q}{\Omega_{\mathrm{BZ}}} \lambda_{\mathbf{q}b} = 2\int_0^\infty\frac{d\omega}{\omega}\alpha^2F(\omega).\]

To describe current relaxation, QTrans uses the velocity factor associated with the momentum relaxation time approximation (MRTA):

\[\eta_{\nu\mathbf{k},\mu\mathbf{k+q}} = 1-\frac{\mathbf{v}_{\nu\mathbf{k}}\cdot \mathbf{v}_{\mu\mathbf{k+q}}}{|\mathbf{v}_{\nu\mathbf{k}}|^2}.\]

For equal initial and final speed, this factor reduces to \(1-\cos\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between the two velocities. It suppresses forward scattering and emphasizes processes that relax the current. Inserting this factor gives

\[\begin{split}\lambda_{\mathrm{tr},\mathbf{q}b} ={}& \frac{2}{\hbar N_F\omega_{\mathbf{q}b}} \sum_{\mu\nu}\int_{\mathrm{BZ}}\frac{d^3k}{\Omega_{\mathrm{BZ}}} |g_{\mu\nu b}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q})|^2 \\ &\times\delta(\varepsilon_{\nu\mathbf{k}}-\varepsilon_F) \delta(\varepsilon_{\mu\mathbf{k+q}}-\varepsilon_F) \eta_{\nu\mathbf{k},\mu\mathbf{k+q}},\end{split}\]

and the transport spectral function is

\[\alpha_{\mathrm{tr}}^2F(\omega) = \frac{1}{2}\sum_b\int_{\mathrm{BZ}} \frac{d^3q}{\Omega_{\mathrm{BZ}}} \omega_{\mathbf{q}b}\lambda_{\mathrm{tr},\mathbf{q}b} \delta(\omega-\omega_{\mathbf{q}b}).\]

Ziman and Allen Estimates

The Ziman-type estimate [4] uses a free-electron Drude prefactor:

\[\rho_{\mathrm{Ziman}}(T) = \frac{4\pi m_e}{n_c e^2 k_{\mathrm{B}}T} \int_0^\infty d\omega\,\hbar\omega\, \alpha_{\mathrm{tr}}^2F(\omega) n(\omega,T)[1+n(\omega,T)],\]

where \(m_e\) is the free-electron mass, \(e>0\) is the elementary charge, \(n_c\) is the total carrier number density per unit volume including both spins, and

\[n(\omega,T)=\frac{1}{\exp[\hbar\omega/(k_{\mathrm{B}}T)]-1}.\]

The Allen-type estimate [5] replaces the free-electron prefactor with a Fermi-surface velocity average:

\[\rho_{\mathrm{Allen}}(T) = \frac{2\pi V_{\mathrm{uc}}} {e^2 N_F\langle v_z^2\rangle k_{\mathrm{B}}T} \int_0^\infty d\omega\,\hbar\omega\, \alpha_{\mathrm{tr}}^2F(\omega) n(\omega,T)[1+n(\omega,T)],\]

where \(V_{\mathrm{uc}}\) is the unit-cell volume and

\[\langle v_z^2\rangle = \frac{1}{N_F}\sum_\nu\int_{\mathrm{BZ}} \frac{d^3k}{\Omega_{\mathrm{BZ}}} v_{\nu\mathbf{k}z}^2\delta(\varepsilon_{\nu\mathbf{k}}-\varepsilon_F).\]

For an isotropic metal, this average is independent of the chosen Cartesian direction. Using \(x=\hbar\omega/(2k_{\mathrm{B}}T)\) and \(n(1+n)=1/(4\sinh^2x)\), an equivalent expression is

\[\rho_{\mathrm{Allen}}(T) = \frac{2\pi V_{\mathrm{uc}}k_{\mathrm{B}}T} {e^2\hbar N_F\langle v_z^2\rangle} \int_0^\infty\frac{d\omega}{\omega} \frac{x^2}{\sinh^2x}\alpha_{\mathrm{tr}}^2F(\omega).\]

For a three-dimensional parabolic free-electron band, \(2N_F\langle v_z^2\rangle/V_{\mathrm{uc}}=n_c/m_e\), so the two prefactors agree.

Note

These scalar estimates use an isotropic transport approximation. The MRTA velocity factor is also an approximation for general multiband Fermi surfaces. Anisotropic transport is better described using the BTE conductivity tensor below. Spin-resolved calculations require consistent spin counting in the spectral function, density of states, and carrier density; the prefactors above assume two equivalent spin channels.

Resistivity from the Conductivity Tensor

The BTE approach gives the conductivity tensor as

\[\sigma_{\alpha\beta}(T) = -\frac{e}{V_{\mathrm{uc}}}\sum_\nu \int_{\mathrm{BZ}}\frac{d^3k}{\Omega_{\mathrm{BZ}}} v_{\nu\mathbf{k}\alpha}\partial_{E_\beta}f_{\nu\mathbf{k}},\]

where \(\partial_{E_\beta}f_{\nu\mathbf{k}}\) is the distribution response at zero electric field. The band sum must include all spin states, or the corresponding spin degeneracy factor must be included explicitly.

The resistivity tensor is the matrix inverse of the conductivity tensor:

\[\boldsymbol{\rho}(T)=\boldsymbol{\sigma}(T)^{-1}, \qquad \rho_{\alpha\beta}(T)=[\boldsymbol{\sigma}(T)^{-1}]_{\alpha\beta}.\]

This relation applies when the conductivity matrix is invertible. Only when that matrix is diagonal does \(\rho_{\alpha\alpha}=1/\sigma_{\alpha\alpha}\) hold component by component. The tensor approach can describe anisotropic metals within the scattering mechanisms and approximations included in the BTE calculation.
